tldr: This paper reports size-dependent melting point depression of charge density waves in 1T-TiSe2 nanoflakes, a condensed matter physics study of electronic phase transitions.
motivation: To investigate whether size effects can influence the melting of electronic ordered states like charge density waves, which is rarely observed due to the small length scales required.
method: Transmission electron microscopy and transport measurements on 1T-TiSe2 nanoflakes of varying thicknesses to observe the charge density wave transition temperature.
result: The charge density wave melting temperature decreases with decreasing flake thickness, demonstrating size-dependent suppression of the ordered phase.
conclusion: Size effects play a significant role in electronic phase transitions, analogous to classical melting point depression, and must be considered in nanoscale correlated systems.

title: Micrometer-range Spin-wave Transport By Incorporating Perpendicular Spins In Artificial Spin Ice
authors: Syamlal Sankaran Kunnath, Mateusz Zelent, Pawel Gruszecki, And Maciej Krawczyk
abstract:

motivation: To explore wave phenomena in artificial spin ice, which are typically limited by weak dipolar coupling.
method: The authors incorporate perpendicular spins to enhance dipolar coupling and enable micrometer-range spin-wave transport, likely using micromagnetic simulations.
result: They demonstrate that perpendicular spins can significantly extend spin-wave propagation distances in artificial spin ice.
conclusion: This approach may enable new magnonic devices but does not directly contribute to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

method: Angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) and scanning photoemission microscopy (SPEM) were used to probe the electronic structure.
result: Partial depletion of Fermi surfaces is observed in the CDW phase, indicating spectral reconstruction.
conclusion: The CDW formation significantly modifies the electronic structure, consistent with a Peierls-like mechanism.

result: Observation of stripe order and its correlation with superconductivity in KTaO3 heterostructures.
conclusion: The percolative pathway provides a mechanism for stripe order and unconventional superconductivity in oxide interfaces.

title: Exchange Monte Carlo For Continuous-space Path Integral Monte Carlo Simulation
authors: Xun Zhao And Synge Todo
abstract:

We present an exchange Monte Carlo (EMC) method designed for application in continuous-space path integral Monte Carlo (PIMC) simulations at finite temperature. Traditional PIMC methods for bosonic systems suffer from long autocorrelation times, particularly when measuring observables affected by pa…


[Phys. Rev. E 113, 065304] Published Fri Jun 05, 2026.
tldr: This paper presents an exchange Monte Carlo method for continuous-space path integral Monte Carlo simulations to reduce autocorrelation times.
motivation: Traditional PIMC methods for bosonic systems suffer from long autocorrelation times, especially for observables affected by permutation sampling.
method: The authors propose an exchange Monte Carlo (EMC) algorithm that swaps configurations between different temperature replicas to improve sampling efficiency in continuous-space PIMC.
result: The EMC method reduces autocorrelation times and improves the accuracy of measured observables in benchmark simulations.
conclusion: The proposed EMC technique is effective for accelerating PIMC simulations of bosonic systems at finite temperature.

title: Diffusion-driven Pattern Formation In An Opinion Dynamical Network Model
authors: Tim Mauch And Thilo Gross

The spatial organization of individuals and their interactions in communities are important factors known to preserve diversity in many complex systems. Inspired by metapopulation models from ecology, we study opinion formation using a network-based approach in which nodes represent communities of i…


[Phys. Rev. E 113, 064302] Published Thu Jun 04, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies opinion formation using a network-based metapopulation model, focusing on spatial pattern formation and diversity preservation.
motivation: Understanding how spatial organization and network structure influence opinion diversity in complex social systems.
method: A network model where nodes represent communities with internal dynamics, coupled via migration-like interactions, analyzed using linear stability analysis and numerical simulations.
result: The model exhibits diffusion-driven pattern formation analogous to Turing patterns, leading to stable spatial heterogeneity in opinions.
conclusion: Spatial coupling and network topology can sustain opinion diversity, with implications for social dynamics and complex systems.

motivation: To understand the phase transition in a technologically relevant ferroelectric polymer.
method: Analytical free-energy model based on Landau theory, incorporating dipole interactions and chain conformations.
result: Predicts transition temperature and polarization as functions of copolymer composition and temperature.
conclusion: The model captures key features of the transition and can guide material design.

title: Externally Driven Condensates Show Translation-induced Polarization, Directed Coalescence, And Anomalous Diffusion In Viscoelastic Media
authors: Andriy Goychuk

tldr: This paper studies phase separation in viscoelastic media under external driving, focusing on polarization, coalescence, and anomalous diffusion.
motivation: Understanding how external fields and viscoelasticity control the organization of phase-separated domains in soft matter and biological systems.
method: Theoretical modeling and numerical simulations of externally driven condensates in viscoelastic media.
result: Translation-induced polarization, directed coalescence, and anomalous diffusion are observed.
conclusion: External driving can be used to control the morphology and dynamics of phase-separated domains in viscoelastic environments.

title: First-passage-time Properties Of Diffusion With A Broad Class Of Stochastic Diffusion Coefficients
authors: Go Uchida, Hiromi Miyoshi, And Hitoshi Washizu

This study investigates the first-passage-time (FPT) properties of particles with a broad class of positive stochastic diffusion coefficients (DCs), representing diffusion in heterogeneous environments or of particles with conformational fluctuations. We demonstrate that for diffusion in a one-dimen…


[Phys. Rev. E 113, 064108] Published Tue Jun 02, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies first-passage-time properties of diffusion with stochastic diffusion coefficients in heterogeneous environments.
motivation: Understanding first-passage times in heterogeneous media is important for transport in disordered systems and biological processes.
method: Analytical and numerical methods are used to derive FPT distributions for a broad class of positive stochastic diffusion coefficients in one dimension.
result: The FPT properties depend on the statistics of the diffusion coefficient, with explicit expressions for certain cases.
conclusion: The work provides a theoretical framework for FPT in heterogeneous diffusion, relevant to statistical physics but not to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Relative-advection-induced Instability In A Reaction-diffusion-advection System
authors: Chuanjun Dai, Ruyi Zhou, Qing Guo, And Min Zhao

The instability mechanism in general reaction-diffusion-advection systems is key to understanding flow-driven self-organization. [Phys. Rev. E 113, 064202] Published Tue Jun 02, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies instability in reaction-diffusion-advection systems, a topic in nonlinear dynamics and pattern formation, unrelated to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.
motivation: Understanding flow-driven self-organization in reaction-diffusion-advection systems is important for biological and chemical pattern formation.
method: The authors derive general conditions for instability in n-dimensional space, termed relative advection instability (RAI), using linear stability analysis.
result: They identify conditions under which advection alone can induce instability, independent of diffusion or reaction parameters.
conclusion: Relative advection instability is a distinct mechanism for pattern formation in advective systems.

title: Resetting-induced Instability In Queues Fed By A Search Process In An Interval
authors: José Giral-Barajas And Paul C. Bressloff
abstract:

Proper management of resources whose arrival and consumption are subject to environmental randomness is an intrinsic process in both natural and artificial systems. This phenomenon can be modeled as a queuing process whose arrival distribution is determined by a search process with stochastic resett…


[Phys. Rev. E 113, 064101] Published Mon Jun 01, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies a queuing model where arrivals are governed by a search process with stochastic resetting, leading to instability.
motivation: To understand how resetting in search processes affects queue stability, relevant to resource management in random environments.
method: Analytical and numerical analysis of a queue fed by a search process with resetting, using generating functions and stability conditions.
result: Resetting can induce instability in the queue even when the underlying search process is stable, depending on resetting rate and queue parameters.
conclusion: Stochastic resetting can destabilize queues, highlighting the need to account for search dynamics in queueing theory.

tldr: A spanning-tree-based framework to quantify allosteric communication pathways and noise suppression in proteins.
motivation: Understanding how multiple communication pathways contribute to signal transmission and noise suppression in protein allostery.

title: Dynamic Similarity Of Vortex Shedding In A Superfluid Flowing Past A Penetrable Obstacle
authors: Junhwan Kwon And Yong-Il Shin

We numerically investigate wake dynamics in a superfluid flowing past a penetrable obstacle. The penetrable obstacle does not fully deplete the density, and we define an effective diameter [MATH] from the Mach-1 contour of the time-averaged irrotational flow around the obstacle, which …


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 023246] Published Fri Jun 05, 2026.
tldr: Numerical study of vortex shedding dynamics in a superfluid flowing past a penetrable obstacle, focusing on dynamic similarity and effective diameter scaling.
motivation: To understand wake dynamics in superfluids with penetrable obstacles, which are relevant to quantum turbulence and superfluid hydrodynamics.
method: Numerical simulations of the Gross-Pitaevskii equation for a superfluid flow past a penetrable obstacle, analyzing vortex shedding patterns and defining an effective diameter from the Mach-1 contour.
result: The vortex shedding frequency scales with the effective diameter, showing dynamic similarity analogous to classical fluids, with a Strouhal number around 0.4.
conclusion: Penetrable obstacles in superfluids exhibit vortex shedding dynamics similar to classical fluids when characterized by an effective diameter, extending the concept of dynamic similarity to quantum fluids.

title: Phenomenology Of Orbital Torque, Pumping, And Mixing Conductance In Metallic Bilayers
authors: Xiaobai Ning, Henri Jaffrès, Weisheng Zhao, And Aurélien Manchon
abstract:
Author(s): Xiaobai Ning, Henri Jaffrès, Weisheng Zhao, and Aurélien Manchon

The conversion between spin and orbital currents is at the origin of the orbital torque and its Onsager reciprocal, the orbital pumping. Here, we propose a phenomenological model to describe the orbital torque in magnetic bilayers composed of an orbital source (i.e., a light metal such as Ti, Ru, ${…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 023239] Published Tue Jun 02, 2026.
tldr: A phenomenological model for orbital torque and pumping in metallic bilayers, focusing on spin-orbit conversion in light metals.
motivation: Understanding orbital-to-spin current conversion is key for spintronic devices, but the paper is purely condensed matter physics without quantum information or thermodynamics.
method: Phenomenological modeling of orbital torque and pumping using mixing conductance concepts.
result: Derives expressions for orbital torque and pumping in magnetic bilayers with an orbital source layer.
conclusion: Provides a framework for orbital torque but does not connect to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: From Knots To Crystals: Machine-learned Potentials For Self-assembling Topological Solitons In Liquid Crystals
authors: Arunkumar Bupathy, Darian Hall, Ivan I. Smalyukh, Gerardo Campos-Villalobos, Rodolfo Subert, And Marjolein Dijkstra
abstract:
Author(s): Arunkumar Bupathy, Darian Hall, Ivan I. Smalyukh, Gerardo Campos-Villalobos, Rodolfo Subert, and Marjolein Dijkstra

Knotted fields in classical and quantum systems have long been recognized for their nontrivial topologies and particlelike behavior, but practical applications have been limited by the difficulty of stabilizing them. Recently, stable knotted solitonic textures—heliknotons—were discovered in chiral l…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 023235] Published Mon Jun 01, 2026.
tldr: This paper uses machine learning to develop interparticle potentials for self-assembling topological solitons (heliknotons) in liquid crystals.
motivation: Stable knotted solitonic textures in liquid crystals have potential applications but are difficult to stabilize and control; the authors aim to enable self-assembly of these structures.
method: They employ machine-learned potentials (likely neural network or Gaussian approximation potentials) trained on molecular dynamics or experimental data to model interactions between heliknotons.
result: The machine-learned potentials successfully reproduce the self-assembly behavior of heliknotons into crystalline and other ordered phases.
conclusion: Machine-learned potentials can be used to design and predict self-assembly of topological solitons, opening avenues for materials with knotted field configurations.

authors: Hongwei Zhang, Chunsheng Wang, Ran Wang, Senyang Pan, Hengning Wang, Jiaqiang Cai, Yonglai Liu, Zhe Qu, Xiangde Zhu, Wei Ning, Chuanying Xi, Jinglei Zhang, Ning Hao, Guolin Zheng, And Mingliang Tian

Local protonic gating in
[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021046] Published Fri May 29, 2026.
tldr: This paper demonstrates a time-reversal symmetric superconducting diode effect in gate-defined homojunctions using local protonic gating.
motivation: To achieve magnetic-field-free control of nonreciprocal critical currents in superconducting diodes, which is important for low-dissipation electronics.
method: The authors use local protonic gating in homojunctions to induce a superconducting diode effect while preserving time-reversal symmetry.
result: They observe a polarity-tunable superconducting diode effect without external magnetic fields.
conclusion: This work provides a general framework for realizing superconducting diodes in gate-defined homojunctions, enabling field-free control of nonreciprocal transport.

title: Robust Orbital-Selective Flat Bands In Layered Transition-Metal Oxyhalides At Room Temperature
authors: Xiangyu Luo, Ludovica Zullo, Sahaj Patel, Dongjin Oh, Willa Mihalyi-Koch, Emma Lian, Jiaruo Li, Qian Song, Asish K. Kundu, Anil Rajapitamahuni, Elio Vescovo, Natalia Olszowska, Rafał Kurleto, Dawid Wutke, Xavier Roy, Giorgio Sangiovanni, And Riccardo Comin
abstract:
Author(s): Xiangyu Luo, Ludovica Zullo, Sahaj Patel, Dongjin Oh, Willa Mihalyi-Koch, Emma Lian, Jiaruo Li, Qian Song, Asish K. Kundu, Anil Rajapitamahuni, Elio Vescovo, Natalia Olszowska, Rafał Kurleto, Dawid Wutke, Xavier Roy, Giorgio Sangiovanni, and Riccardo Comin

Angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy of layered transition-metal oxyhalides reveals intrinsic flat bands that remain stable at room temperature, providing a tunable platform for investigating strongly correlated electron states.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021041] Published Thu May 21, 2026.
tldr: This paper reports the discovery of robust orbital-selective flat bands in layered transition-metal oxyhalides at room temperature, characterized by angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy.
motivation: Flat bands in strongly correlated materials can host exotic quantum phases, but many are only stable at low temperatures. The authors aim to find a room-temperature platform for studying such phenomena.
method: The authors synthesize layered transition-metal oxyhalides and use angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) to measure the electronic band structure, revealing flat bands that are stable at room temperature.
result: Intrinsic flat bands are observed that remain stable at room temperature, providing a tunable platform for investigating strongly correlated electron states.
conclusion: These materials offer a promising system for exploring flat-band physics and strongly correlated phenomena without the need for cryogenic conditions.

title: Elastic And Structural Anisotropy In Silica Thin Films For Gravitational-Wave Detectors
authors: Brenda Bracco, Michele Magnozzi, Stefano Colace, Maurizio Canepa, Giulio Favaro, Marco Bazzan, Massimo Granata, David Hofman, Alessandro Di Michele, Laura Silenzi, Gianpietro Cagnoli, Giovanni Carlotti, Paola Sassi, And Silvia Corezzi
abstract:
Author(s): Brenda Bracco, Michele Magnozzi, Stefano Colace, Maurizio Canepa, Giulio Favaro, Marco Bazzan, Massimo Granata, David Hofman, Alessandro Di Michele, Laura Silenzi, Gianpietro Cagnoli, Giovanni Carlotti, Paola Sassi, and Silvia Corezzi

Researchers find that silica films in mirror coatings of gravitational-wave detectors have hidden anisotropy that resists standard heat treatment. This discovery informs coating design and deposition and postprocessing strategies aimed at reducing thermal noise.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021036] Published Fri May 15, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies elastic and structural anisotropy in silica thin films used in gravitational-wave detector mirror coatings, focusing on thermal noise reduction.
motivation: Thermal noise in mirror coatings limits the sensitivity of gravitational-wave detectors; understanding and mitigating anisotropy in silica films could improve performance.
method: The authors characterize the elastic and structural properties of silica thin films using experimental techniques to reveal hidden anisotropy and test the effects of heat treatment.
result: Silica films exhibit hidden anisotropy that resists standard heat treatment, impacting their mechanical properties.
conclusion: The findings inform coating design and postprocessing strategies to reduce thermal noise in gravitational-wave detectors.

title: Intertwined Polar, Chiral, And Ferro-Rotational Orders In A Homo-Ferro-Rotational Insulator
authors: Weizhe Zhang, June Ho Yeo, Xiaoyu Guo, Tony Chiang, Nishkarsh Agarwal, John T. Heron, Kai Sun, Junjie Yang, Sang-Wook Cheong, Youngjun Ahn, And Liuyan Zhao

Multimodal optical characterization of Ni
[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021030] Published Fri May 08, 2026.
tldr: This paper reports the observation of intertwined polar, chiral, and ferro-rotational orders in a bulk insulator using multimodal optical characterization.
motivation: To understand the coupling between multiple ferroic orders and the formation of complex domain walls in materials with ferro-rotational order.
method: Multimodal optical characterization techniques (e.g., second harmonic generation, optical rotation) were used to probe the polar, chiral, and ferro-rotational domains in Ni₃TeO₆.
result: A uniform ferro-rotational state is identified that couples polarity and chirality, leading to complex mixed-type domain walls.
conclusion: The findings reveal a new type of multiferroic order and provide insights into the interplay between different ferroic orders.

title: Active Hydrodynamic Theory Of Euchromatin And Heterochromatin
authors: S. Alex Rautu, Alexandra Zidovska, David Saintillan, And Michael J. Shelley
abstract:
Author(s): S. Alex Rautu, Alexandra Zidovska, David Saintillan, and Michael J. Shelley

Researchers develop a theoretical framework that shows how mechanical forces and flows drive the spatial segregation and nucleus-wide patterning of chromatin in cells.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021009] Published Thu Apr 09, 2026.
tldr: Develops an active hydrodynamic theory to explain the spatial segregation of euchromatin and heterochromatin in the cell nucleus.
motivation: Understanding how mechanical forces and flows drive chromatin organization is crucial for cell biology, but the paper does not connect to quantum information or thermodynamics.
method: The authors formulate a continuum active fluid model incorporating chromatin activity, viscoelasticity, and hydrodynamic interactions.
result: The model predicts spontaneous segregation and patterning of chromatin domains driven by active stresses.
conclusion: Mechanical forces alone can explain large-scale chromatin organization, offering a physical mechanism for nuclear architecture.

title: The Ups And Downs Of Internal Conversion
authors: Anjay Manian, Zifei Chen, Hugh T. Sullivan, And Salvy P. Russo
abstract:
Author(s): Anjay Manian, Zifei Chen, Hugh T. Sullivan, and Salvy P. Russo

This review examines the theoretical methods used to describe the photophysical process of internal conversion in quantum systems. These models explore all facets of the nonradiative mechanism, and the review presents an outlook on how they can be incorporated in studies relevant to applications, for example, in photonics and energy harvesting.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 035003] Published Tue Sep 16, 2025.
tldr: A review of theoretical methods for internal conversion in quantum systems, focusing on nonradiative transitions and their applications in photonics and energy harvesting.
motivation: Internal conversion is a key photophysical process affecting the efficiency of light-emitting devices and solar energy conversion, yet its theoretical description remains challenging.
method: The paper reviews various theoretical models, including nonadiabatic dynamics, Fermi's golden rule, and mixed quantum-classical approaches, to describe internal conversion.
result: The review summarizes the strengths and limitations of current methods and identifies open questions in the field.
conclusion: Improved theoretical methods for internal conversion are needed to better predict and optimize photophysical properties in materials for photonics and energy harvesting.

title: Continuous Thermochemical Sources Of AlF Molecules
authors: Pulkit Kukreja, Priyansh Agarwal, Maximilian Doppelbauer, Jionghao Cai, Xiangyue Liu, Eduardo Padilla, Sebastian Kray, Henrik Haak, Russell Thomas, Stefan Truppe, Boris G Sartakov, Gerard Meijer And Sid Wright
abstract: The AlF molecule, currently subject to laser cooling and trapping efforts, has the advantage that it can be efficiently produced in a thermochemical reaction between sublimated aluminum trifluoride and aluminum metal. Here we present a series of experiments with continuous molecular beam sources of AlF, utilizing this reaction. We demonstrate a compact AlF molecular beam oven whose total far-field brightness is molecules per steradian per second at 923 K, just below the melting temperature of aluminum metal. The continuous output from the oven begins to exceed the peak brightness of a jet-cooled, ablation-based supersonic AlF source for the , level, and we obtain an excellent signal-to-noise ratio with the oven in pulsed laser ionization spectroscopy experiments. By delivering flux from the oven into a cryogenic Ne buffer gas cell, we lower the rotational temperature of the beam to around 30 K and reduce its most probable forward velocity from 600 m s to 200 m s . In addition, we demonstrate that AlF can be made in a simple dispenser package, and observe that molecules thermalize to the laboratory temperature after colliding with vacuum chamber walls of the experiment. The resulting transient AlF vapor may enable direct loading of a molecular magneto-optical trap.
tldr: This paper presents experimental development of continuous thermochemical sources for AlF molecules, focusing on molecular beam brightness and cooling for laser cooling and trapping.
motivation: AlF molecules are promising for laser cooling and trapping, but efficient and continuous sources are needed for advanced experiments.
method: The authors construct a compact AlF molecular beam oven using a thermochemical reaction between sublimated AlF3 and Al metal, and also demonstrate a dispenser package source. They characterize beam brightness, rotational temperature, and velocity using spectroscopy.
result: The oven achieves a total far-field brightness of 10^11 molecules/sr/s at 923 K, exceeding the peak brightness of an ablation-based supersonic source for the v=0, J=1 level. Cryogenic buffer gas cooling reduces rotational temperature to ~30 K and forward velocity from 600 m/s to 200 m/s.
conclusion: Continuous thermochemical sources can produce bright, slow AlF beams suitable for loading magneto-optical traps, advancing molecular quantum science.

title: Evolutionary Vaccination Dynamics Under Higher-order Reinforcement Pressure
authors: Yikang Lu, Ying Wang, Alfonso de Miguel-Arribas, Lei Shi And Yamir Moreno
abstract: Vaccination games in higher-order settings remain underexplored, despite their importance in shaping opinions and collective decisions. Here, we introduce a parsimonious behavioral-epidemiological model to evaluate how peer reinforcement influences vaccination uptake. The framework consists of a two-layer multiplex: an epidemic layer governed by the susceptible-infected-recovered process on a square lattice, and a behavioral layer represented by a hypergraph of triadic interactions. Individuals update their vaccination strategy via imitation, modulated by a reinforcement modulation parameter when local agreement with a like-minded peer is present. We find that higher-order structure alone induces clusters of vaccinated individuals that act as protective barriers. Small but nonzero values of ( ) maximize vaccination coverage and suppress outbreaks, while both the limiting case and larger values ( ) reduce uptake. This non-monotonic effect suggests that excessively strong local inhibition suppresses adaptability, whereas weaker inhibition facilitates the re-emergence of non-vaccinators. Our work bridges complex contagion theory with evolutionary game dynamics, offering insights into how contact structure and peer reinforcement jointly shape vaccination behavior.
tldr: This paper studies vaccination behavior on a multiplex network with higher-order interactions, using evolutionary game theory and epidemic modeling.
motivation: To understand how higher-order social reinforcement influences vaccination uptake and epidemic outcomes.
method: A two-layer multiplex model with an SIR epidemic on a square lattice and a hypergraph for triadic social interactions, where individuals update vaccination strategies via imitation with reinforcement modulation.
result: Higher-order structure creates vaccinated clusters; small reinforcement maximizes coverage and suppresses outbreaks, while too strong or too weak reinforcement reduces uptake.
conclusion: The non-monotonic effect of reinforcement highlights the importance of contact structure and peer influence in shaping vaccination behavior.

title: Crystallography-driven Molecularization Of A Two-dimensional Spin- 3 / ...
authors: Hari Borutta, Tobias Müller, Ronny Thomale, Harald O Jeschke And Yasir Iqbal
abstract: Large-spin two-dimensional magnets are generally expected to develop conventional long-range order once the dominant exchange scale becomes appreciable. The layered spin- maple-leaf compound Na Mn O defies this expectation: despite sizable antiferromagnetic interactions and no evident disorder, it exhibits no magnetic ordering and displays two well-separated thermodynamic crossover scales. We show that this behavior originates from a crystallography-driven molecularization of the magnetic degrees of freedom. The low-symmetry structure partitions the Mn sublattice into inequivalent exchange pathways, generating a pronounced hierarchy that nearly isolates antiferromagnetic hexagons. Magnetic correlations therefore develop in two stages: first within individual hexagons at a scale set by the dominant exchange, and only at much lower temperatures do frustrated inter-hexagon couplings attempt to establish coherence across the lattice. While isolated hexagons reproduce the two-step thermodynamic structure, the experimentally relevant temperature scales emerge only once the hexagons are embedded in the frustrated two-dimensional network. The resulting quantum ground state is magnetically disordered, characterized by strong intra-hexagon correlations and rapidly decaying inter-hexagon correlations. These results identify crystallographic inequivalence as a materials-level mechanism for stabilizing molecularized and quantum-disordered states even in large-spin two-dimensional magnets.
tldr: This paper explains the absence of magnetic order in a large-spin 2D magnet via crystallography-driven molecularization into weakly coupled antiferromagnetic hexagons.
motivation: To understand why the layered spin-3/2 compound Na2Mn3O7 does not order magnetically despite strong antiferromagnetic interactions and no disorder.
method: The authors use density functional theory (DFT) to extract exchange couplings, then model the system with classical Monte Carlo and exact diagonalization of small clusters.
result: The low-symmetry crystal structure creates a hierarchy of exchanges that nearly isolate antiferromagnetic hexagons, leading to two-stage thermal crossover and a quantum-disordered ground state.
conclusion: Crystallographic inequivalence can stabilize molecularized, quantum-disordered states in large-spin 2D magnets, offering a new materials design principle.

title: Computing Phase Diagrams Using A Convex Hull Algorithm
authors: E. D. Young C. P. Dullemond
abstract: ArXiv:2606.09921v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a simple universal computational algorithm for computing compositional phase diagrams of rocks and their melts at given temperature and pressure. It makes use of the mathematical concept of the convex hull of a set of points in the space spanned by the composition and the Gibbs free energy. All the complexities of determining the stability or separation of phases, the localization and orientation of tie lines, as well as the determination of characteristic points, curves and surfaces such as the solidus, liquidus, solvus, and the eutectic/peritectic points etc, are taken care of by the algorithm that computes the convex hull, supplemented with an algorithm to physically classify the resulting simplices. For the convex hull computation, the publicly available Qhull package can be used, which is available in SciPy. This makes this method accessible and intuitive for a broad set of scientific and educational applications. Although the method is not practical for systems of a large number of components, it is remarkably stable and efficient for systems of up to four. We present our implementation of the method as a publicly available Python package.
tldr: A computational algorithm for computing compositional phase diagrams of rocks and melts using convex hull methods.
motivation: To provide a simple, universal, and accessible method for computing phase diagrams in petrology and materials science.
method: Uses the convex hull of points in composition-Gibbs free energy space, supplemented with a classification algorithm for simplices, implemented via Qhull in SciPy.
result: The algorithm efficiently computes phase diagrams for systems with up to four components, determining stability, tie lines, and characteristic points.
conclusion: The method is stable and efficient for small-component systems, and the implementation is publicly available as a Python package.

title: Intrinsic Plasmon Canalization In The Biaxial Van Der Waals Crystal MoOCl$_2$
authors: Farid Aghashirinov, Andrea Mancini, Lin Nan, Giacomo Venturi, Bettina Frank, Harald Giessen, Antonio Ambrosio
abstract: ArXiv:2606.10534v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Anisotropic polaritons in low-symmetry crystals allow for subwavelength confinement and directional routing of light. The most extreme form of such anisotropy arises at the topological transition between elliptical and hyperbolic dispersion, where the isofrequency contours collapse into parallel lines and polaritons propagate in a diffractionless, beam-like fashion. This canalization regime has previously been accessed through twisted heterostructures or engineered metasurfaces. Here we show that natural canalization can be achieved without any fabrication or structuring by exploiting the intrinsic elliptical-to-hyperbolic transition in the van der Waals crystal MoOCl[MATH] at room temperature. Using near-field imaging, we directly visualize plasmon-polariton canalization emerging at the low-loss Drude crossing point along the [010] crystal axis. Owing to the moderate slope of the Drude permittivity, the resulting polaritons remain highly directional across a broad spectral window. This weak dispersion also enables robust thickness-dependent tuning, and we demonstrate, both experimentally and theoretically, that the canalization wavelength can be adjusted by more than 1 {\mu}m simply by varying the flake thickness. This work brings canalized polariton propagation into the 4.5 - 6 {\mu}m range, beyond the frequency limits of phonon-polariton platforms and overlapping with important molecular vibrations, opening new opportunities for mid-IR nanophotonics and sensing.
tldr: This paper demonstrates intrinsic plasmon canalization in the biaxial van der Waals crystal MoOCl2, enabling directional mid-infrared polariton propagation without external structuring.
motivation: Canalized polariton propagation is typically achieved via twisted heterostructures or metasurfaces; this work aims to realize it naturally in a single material for simpler mid-IR nanophotonics.
method: Near-field imaging is used to visualize plasmon-polariton canalization at the Drude crossing point along the [010] crystal axis, supported by theoretical modeling of permittivity and thickness-dependent tuning.
result: Canalization is observed across a broad spectral window (4.5–6 μm), with wavelength tunability over 1 μm by varying flake thickness.
conclusion: MoOCl2 provides a natural platform for canalized polaritons, extending the operating range to mid-IR molecular vibrations and enabling applications in sensing and nanophotonics.

title: Length-dependent Swir Upconversion Spectral Response Of Noncritically Phase-matched Ktp Crystals
authors: Xiao-Hua Wang, Chang-Hao Min, Yin-Hai Li, Zhi-Yuan Zhou, Bao-Sen Shi
abstract: ArXiv:2606.10695v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Noncritically phase-matched KTP crystals are attractive for short-wave infrared upconversion detection because they support large-aperture bulk operation, avoid walk-off, and relax the angular-alignment requirement. Here, we characterize how the crystal length affects the external upconversion spectral response of NCPM KTP crystals. A calibrated Czerny--Turner monochromator is used to measure the normalized external responses of 0.5, 1.0, and 2.0 mm crystals, which are compared with theoretical quantum-efficiency spectra calculated from the phase-matching model. As the crystal length increases, the response evolves from a broad profile to a more pronounced double-peak profile. A representative pump-power measurement is also performed to evaluate the system-level external quantum efficiency. These results provide guidance for selecting the crystal length in SWIR upconversion detection systems using NCPM KTP crystals.
tldr: This paper experimentally characterizes the length-dependent upconversion spectral response of noncritically phase-matched KTP crystals for SWIR detection.
motivation: To understand how crystal length affects the spectral response of NCPM KTP crystals used in short-wave infrared upconversion detection, which is important for optimizing detection systems.
method: The authors used a calibrated Czerny-Turner monochromator to measure the normalized external spectral response of 0.5, 1.0, and 2.0 mm KTP crystals and compared with theoretical quantum-efficiency spectra from a phase-matching model.
result: As crystal length increases, the spectral response evolves from a broad profile to a more pronounced double-peak profile. A representative pump-power measurement was also performed to evaluate system-level external quantum efficiency.
conclusion: The results provide guidance for selecting crystal length in SWIR upconversion detection systems using NCPM KTP crystals.

title: A Modular Structure Theorem For Minimal Periodic Decompositions And Periodicity Of Configurations With $P_{\eta}(4,n) \leq 4n$
authors: E. Garibaldi C. F. Colle
abstract: ArXiv:2606.10193v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Nivat's conjecture asserts that every two-dimensional configuration [MATH] whose rectangular pattern complexity satisfies [MATH] for some [MATH] is periodic. A theorem of Cyr and Kra establishes the conjecture in the short-rectangle case [MATH], with [MATH]. Using the algebraic framework of Kari-Szabados and recent advances on periodic decompositions and one-sided nonexpansive directions , we extend the Cyr-Kra result to the case [MATH]: every configuration satisfying this complexity bound is periodic. The key new ingredient is an intermediate structural theorem of independent interest: for any non-periodic configuration with low convex pattern complexity and integer-valued alphabet [MATH] contained in [MATH], there exist a configuration [MATH] in the orbit closure of [MATH], a [MATH]-minimal periodic decomposition [MATH], a prime [MATH] with [MATH], and pairs of disjoint half-planes [MATH] such that the reductions modulo [MATH] of the components [MATH] are fully periodic on [MATH] and on [MATH] simultaneously, for each [MATH].
tldr: Proves a modular structure theorem for minimal periodic decompositions and extends a result on periodicity of low-complexity 2D configurations.
motivation: To prove Nivat's conjecture for a specific complexity bound and to provide a structural theorem for non-periodic configurations.
method: Uses algebraic framework of Kari-Szabados and recent advances on periodic decompositions and one-sided nonexpansive directions.
result: Extends Cyr-Kra result to the case where pattern complexity is at most 4n, showing every such configuration is periodic.
conclusion: The structural theorem is of independent interest and the periodicity result advances understanding of low-complexity configurations.

title: Intrinsic Footpoint-invariant Riemannian Cross-covariance
authors: Carlos Soto, Cheng Wang, Zipan Huang, Xiaoyu Chen
abstract: ArXiv:2606.10212v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Covariance estimation yields a fundamental second-order statistic underlying representation learning, dimension reduction, and dependence modeling. While covariance has been well understood in Euclidean spaces, it is ill-defined for random objects residing on nonlinear Riemannian manifolds, which increasingly arise in modern machine learning applications involving shapes, symmetric positive definite (SPD) matrices, etc. This paper introduces an intrinsic Riemannian cross-covariance for manifold-valued random objects. Our approach defines covariance and correlation by transporting local variations to a common tangent space via parallel transport, yielding a second-order descriptor that is independent of arbitrary coordinate choices. We establish that the proposed covariance inherits desirable properties of its Euclidean counterparts and characterize its asymptotic behavior. Numerical studies on spheres and SPD manifolds, together with real-data experiments on heart valve shapes in Kendall's shape space, demonstrate the effectiveness of our estimators and verify the stated properties. Our results position the Riemannian covariance as a fundamental tool for second-order learning and analysis in non-Euclidean representation spaces.
tldr: This paper introduces an intrinsic Riemannian cross-covariance for manifold-valued data, focusing on statistical learning on nonlinear spaces.
motivation: Covariance estimation is fundamental in Euclidean spaces but ill-defined for data on Riemannian manifolds, which arise in modern ML applications.
method: The authors define covariance by transporting local variations to a common tangent space via parallel transport, ensuring coordinate independence.
result: The proposed covariance inherits Euclidean properties and is validated on spheres, SPD manifolds, and real heart valve shape data.
conclusion: The Riemannian covariance provides a fundamental tool for second-order learning in non-Euclidean spaces.

title: Constructive Versions Of Ekeland's Variational Principle
authors: Douglas S. Bridges
abstract: ArXiv:2606.10339v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Building on preliminary results about lower sections of real-valued functions on a metric space, we provide a constructive counterpart of Ekeland's theorem on the approximate optimisation of real-valued functions.
tldr: This paper provides a constructive (Bishop-style) version of Ekeland's variational principle, a result in functional analysis and optimization.
motivation: Ekeland's variational principle is a key tool in nonlinear analysis and optimization, but its classical proof uses non-constructive reasoning. The authors aim to provide a fully constructive counterpart.
method: The paper builds on preliminary results about lower sections of real-valued functions on a metric space, then uses constructive analysis techniques to prove the variational principle.
result: A constructive version of Ekeland's variational principle is established, ensuring that the approximate minimizer can be found algorithmically.
conclusion: The work contributes to constructive mathematics by making a fundamental optimization theorem computationally meaningful.

title: A Mean-Field Analysis Of Multi-Head Self-Attention Under Cross-Entropy Training
authors: Hongfwei Yuan Cheng Huan
abstract: ArXiv:2606.10469v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper develops a mean-field theory for a simplified single-layer causal multi-head self-attention model trained by cross-entropy minimization. Each attention head is treated as a particle in parameter space, and the empirical law of the heads is used as the large-head state variable. In the infinite-head limit, the averaged attention logits define a risk functional on probability measures, whose first variation generates a nonlinear Wasserstein gradient-flow equation. Unlike classical mean-field analyses of shallow networks that often focus on square-loss regression, the present model contains the softmax residual from the cross-entropy objective and the query-key-value structure of masked self-attention. We prove a static finite-head approximation bound for the optimal risk, characterize global minimizers through a variational support condition, and establish a quantitative finite-time propagation-of-chaos estimate comparing finite-head stochastic gradient descent with the limiting PDE. We then study the long-time behavior of the PDE: energy dissipation, convergence to the stationary set under compactness, convergence to a single stationary measure under topological or Kurdyka--{\L}ojasiewicz assumptions, and explicit convergence rates under gradient-domination conditions. Finally, we prove local exponential stability under a Wasserstein strong-monotonicity condition and give verifiable stability and instability criteria for Dirac stationary measures. The results provide a rigorous baseline mean-field framework for attention-head training and clarify the additional compactness, landscape, and curvature assumptions needed to pass from stationarity to convergence and stability.
tldr: A mean-field analysis of multi-head self-attention under cross-entropy training, focusing on the infinite-head limit and gradient-flow dynamics.
motivation: To provide a rigorous theoretical framework for understanding the training dynamics of attention mechanisms in transformers, which are widely used in machine learning.
method: Treats each attention head as a particle, derives a Wasserstein gradient-flow PDE in the infinite-head limit, and proves finite-head approximation bounds and propagation-of-chaos estimates.
result: Establishes convergence properties of the PDE, including energy dissipation, convergence to stationary measures, and local exponential stability under certain conditions.
conclusion: The work provides a baseline mean-field framework for attention-head training, clarifying assumptions needed for convergence and stability.

title: Two Integral Sliding-Window Inequalities For Maximal Convolutions
authors: Cheng Li Gangsong Leng
abstract: ArXiv:2606.10518v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove two sliding-window inequalities for maximal convolutions. The first concerns the multiplicative maximal convolution. If [MATH] and [MATH] are nonnegative continuous functions on [MATH] and [MATH], respectively, define \[ h(x)=\max_{} f(u)g(x-u),\qquad 0\le x\le A+B. \] Then there exists a window [MATH] of length [MATH] such that \[ \frac1B\int_a^{a+B}h(x)\,dx\ge \left(\frac1A\int_0^A f(x)\,dx\right) \left(\frac1B\int_0^B g(x)\,dx\right). \] The second concerns the additive maximal convolution. Let [MATH] and [MATH] be nonnegative continuous functions on [MATH], and define \[ H(x)=\max_{}\{f(u)+g(x-u)\},\qquad 0\le x\le 2C. \] Then, for every [MATH], there exists a window [MATH] of length [MATH] such that \[ \left(\int_a^{a+C}H(x)^p\,dx\right)^{1/p} \ge \left(\int_0^C f(x)^p\,dx\right)^{1/p} + \left(\int_0^C g(x)^p\,dx\right)^{1/p}. \] We also record discrete analogues. The main point is that, in one-dimensional maximal-convolution settings, certain global Brunn--Minkowski or Pr\'ekopa--Leindler type phenomena admit natural sliding-window localizations.
tldr: The paper proves integral sliding-window inequalities for maximal convolutions, which are mathematical results in analysis and convex geometry.
motivation: To establish local versions of Brunn-Minkowski type inequalities for maximal convolutions, extending global results to sliding-window settings.
method: The authors use analytical techniques to derive two inequalities: one for multiplicative maximal convolution and one for additive maximal convolution, along with discrete analogues.
result: They show that for certain maximal convolutions, there exists a window of given length such that an integral inequality holds, relating averages of the convolution to averages of the original functions.
conclusion: The work provides new local inequalities in the context of maximal convolutions, contributing to the theory of inequalities and convex geometry.

title: On Concatenation Of Matrices For Reversible Linear Codes Over A Finite Commutative Ring And Applications To Dna Codes
authors: Satyadeep Pandey Avanish Kumar Chaturvedi
abstract: ArXiv:2606.10633v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we develop a generalized framework for constructing reversible linear, reversible self dual and reversible DNA codes using a matrix-theoretic approach based on involutory matrices. The proposed concatenation scheme gives a large class of generator matrices and yields codes with good parameters. The construction is carried out at the level of linear codes and then extended to DNA codes. Using a matrix product approach, we provide a unified method for analysis and proof. Further, we resolve an open problem raised by Oztas et.al. and also we correct and improve some results of them.
tldr: This paper develops a matrix-theoretic framework for constructing reversible linear codes over finite commutative rings and applies it to DNA codes.
motivation: To generalize and improve methods for constructing reversible and DNA codes using involutory matrices and concatenation.
method: Uses matrix concatenation based on involutory matrices to generate reversible linear, self-dual, and DNA codes, with proofs via matrix product approach.
result: Provides a large class of generator matrices yielding codes with good parameters, resolves an open problem, and corrects previous results.
conclusion: The proposed framework offers a unified and improved method for constructing reversible and DNA codes.

title: Improved Bounds For Numerical Radius And $a$-numerical Radius In ${C}^*$-algebras
authors: Saikat Mahapatra, Arobinda Ghosh, Riddhick Birbonshi
abstract: ArXiv:2606.10659v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this article, we derive several significant upper bounds for the numerical radius and [MATH]-numerical radius of an element in a [MATH]-algebra by improving inequalities for positive linear functionals. Our findings refine and generalize the existing inequalities. Furthermore, we introduce a new notion to derive improved upper bounds of the numerical radius for an element in a [MATH]-algebra using the Moore-Penrose inverse.
tldr: The paper derives improved upper bounds for numerical radius and a-numerical radius in C*-algebras using inequalities for positive linear functionals and Moore-Penrose inverse.
motivation: To refine and generalize existing inequalities for numerical radius in C*-algebras, which is a topic in functional analysis and operator theory.
method: The authors use algebraic manipulations and properties of positive linear functionals, along with the Moore-Penrose inverse, to derive new bounds.
result: Several new upper bounds for numerical radius and a-numerical radius are obtained, improving upon known results.
conclusion: The findings contribute to the theory of numerical radius in C*-algebras but have no direct connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: The Chronicles Of Radio Frequency Fingerprinting
authors: Abdul Aziz, Ingrid Huso, Savio Sciancalepore, Gabriele Oligeri
abstract: ArXiv:2606.10031v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Radio Frequency Fingerprinting (RFF) has evolved from an early idea for radar emitter identification into a broad research field for wireless device identification and spectrum monitoring for security. Rather than presenting a conventional literature survey, this work provides a critical historical analysis of RFF organized around the field's major conceptual paradigm shifts from 1993 to 2026. We discuss the evolution of RFF across its fundamental methodological phases, beginning with early transient-based approaches, in which transmitter turn-on behavior, unintentional modulation, and hardware nonlinearities were treated as the primary fingerprint sources. We then examine the transition to digital communications, during which attention shifted to steady-state impairments and to engineered features extracted from signals. Next, we discuss the Machine Learning period, which standardized the RFF workflow around feature extraction, dimensionality reduction, and supervised classification, followed by the Deep Learning period, in which representation learning from raw IQ samples significantly improved performance and expanded the application space. Beyond a chronological list of methods and best practices, this paper critically examines the changing assumptions and persistent limitations that have driven these transitions. We highlight the central challenges that continue to shape the field, including channel dependence, receiver sensitivity, limited dataset realism, poor cross-domain generalization, open-set recognition, and adversarial robustness. By organizing more than three decades of work into a coherent narrative, this paper clarifies the evolution of RFF, identifies persistent limitations, and outlines the key research directions required to move the field toward dependable real-world adoption.
tldr: A historical survey of radio frequency fingerprinting (RFF) for wireless device identification, covering paradigm shifts from 1993 to 2026.
motivation: To provide a critical historical analysis of RFF, clarifying its evolution and persistent limitations to guide future research.
method: Organizes RFF research into conceptual phases: transient-based, steady-state, machine learning, and deep learning, with critical examination of assumptions and challenges.
result: Identifies key challenges such as channel dependence, dataset realism, cross-domain generalization, and adversarial robustness.
conclusion: RFF has matured but still faces fundamental obstacles; future work must address these for dependable real-world adoption.

title: Graft: Graphlet-Triggered Backdoor Attack On GNN-Based Hardware Security Systems
authors: Sai Manoj Pudukotai Dinakarrao Sanaz Kazemi Abharian
abstract: ArXiv:2606.10163v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The globalization of the integrated circuit (IC) supply chain increases the risk of security threats, such as hardware Trojans (HTs) and the theft of intellectual property (IP). Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), among the most powerful deep learning methods for processing graph-structured data, have been widely adopted to detect such threats. However, GNNs are susceptible to backdoor attacks that can maliciously manipulate output predictions toward an adversarial target. These attacks are not only difficult to detect but also compromise the integrity of GNN-based security systems. Most prior work embeds backdoor triggers using randomly generated subgraphs or gradient-guided generative subgraphs. However, such triggers are impractical for GNN-based hardware security applications as they do not guarantee the preservation of circuit functionality. In this paper, we propose GRAFT, a graph let-triggered backdoor attack targeting GNN-based hardware security. GRAFT embeds graphlet-based triggers at either the register-transfer level (RTL) or gate level of the design while preserving the circuit 's original function. We evaluate GRAFT on the ISCAS-85 and TrustHub datasets. Our experimental results demonstrate that GRAFT can effectively evade HT detection and IP piracy detection, achieving an attack success rate (ASR) of up to 100%.
tldr: This paper proposes a graphlet-triggered backdoor attack on GNN-based hardware security systems, focusing on hardware Trojan detection and IP piracy.
motivation: GNN-based hardware security systems are vulnerable to backdoor attacks, and existing triggers are impractical as they do not preserve circuit functionality.
method: The authors embed graphlet-based triggers at RTL or gate level while preserving the circuit's original function, and evaluate on ISCAS-85 and TrustHub datasets.
result: The attack achieves up to 100% attack success rate in evading HT detection and IP piracy detection.
conclusion: GRAFT demonstrates a practical backdoor attack that compromises GNN-based hardware security, highlighting the need for robust defenses.

title: When Vr Meets Bci: (Un)Observable Brainwave-aware Privacy Reconstruction In The Metaverse Via Unrestricted Inbuilt Motion Sensors
authors: Tao Ni, Zehua Sun, Qingchuan Zhao, Wei-Bin Lee, Cong Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2606.10502v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Metaverse devices, such as virtual reality (VR), have seen substantial development and widespread applications in numerous areas. Although recent studies have revealed privacy leakages in VR, these vulnerabilities were limited in the scope of observable behaviors in virtual scenes (e.g., what a user is seeing). In this work, we uncover the feasibility of going beyond the scope of observable user behaviors to unobservable brain EEG-correlated representations (e.g., what a user is perceiving) by leveraging unrestricted motion sensors in VR headsets to reconstruct brain EEG signals, a seemingly neglected but promising vector. The insight is that the inbuilt motion sensors (e.g., accelerometers) in the VR headset can capture subtle vibrations induced by pupillary responses, which are highly correlated with users' visual stimuli and in-brain perceptions. Therefore, we design and implement BraVeSpy to systematically investigate and demonstrate the feasibility of this severe privacy leakage originating from brain EEG-correlated representations reconstructed from variations of inbuilt motion sensors. Our extensive evaluation results from different VR devices show that BraVeSpy, for the first time in the Metaverse, can reveal unobservable privacy, where we successfully unveiled perceptive images in the brain with 52.0%-67.2% accuracy. In particular, we also find that BraVeSpy outperforms the current approaches that are limited to coarse-grained inference of observable behaviors and achieves over 85.0% accuracy in inferring user activity-related sensitive information, such as fingerprinting websites, apps, and streaming videos, and over 96.0% accuracy in user de-anonymization, gaze movement tracking, and virtual keystroke inference.
tldr: This paper demonstrates a privacy attack in VR that reconstructs brain EEG signals from motion sensor vibrations, unrelated to quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: To show that VR motion sensors can capture brainwave-correlated vibrations, enabling privacy leakage beyond observable behaviors.
method: Uses accelerometers in VR headsets to measure subtle vibrations from pupillary responses, then reconstructs EEG-correlated signals to infer visual stimuli and user activities.
result: Achieves 52-67% accuracy in reconstructing perceptive images and over 85% accuracy in inferring activities like website fingerprinting and keystroke inference.
conclusion: VR motion sensors pose a severe privacy risk by enabling brainwave-aware reconstruction, highlighting the need for countermeasures.

title: A Deployment-Oriented Framework For Explainable AI-Assisted eBPF/XDP Mitigation At The IoT Edge
authors: Abdurrahman Tolay
abstract: ArXiv:2606.10508v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Internet of Things (IoT) deployments combine heterogeneous, resource-constrained devices with weak security configurations, exposed services, limited logging, patching constraints, and long lifecycles. Signature- and threshold-based controls remain useful baselines, but they are insufficient as standalone mechanisms in dynamic IoT networks. Likewise, offline artificial intelligence (AI) benchmark performance alone does not establish operational deployability. This article presents a conceptual framework and research agenda for a Linux-based IoT edge gateway that combines resource-aware flow-level AI-assisted risk scoring, event-level explainability, and bounded mitigation through eBPF/XDP. The controller applies reversible, time-limited actions subject to critical-device safeguards, updates packet-level enforcement state, and records structured logs. The architecture separates complex reasoning and policy control in user space from concise packet-handling decisions in the kernel. It also defines a future hardware-aware evaluation pathway covering detection quality, resource cost, response timing, rollback behaviour, and legitimate-traffic preservation. The paper does not report new experimental meas.
tldr: A conceptual framework for AI-assisted mitigation at the IoT edge using eBPF/XDP, with no experimental results.
motivation: IoT devices are vulnerable and traditional security measures are insufficient; AI can help but must be deployable on resource-constrained hardware.
method: Proposes a Linux-based IoT edge gateway architecture combining flow-level AI risk scoring, event-level explainability, and eBPF/XDP for bounded mitigation.
result: No experimental results are reported; the paper presents only a conceptual framework and future evaluation pathway.
conclusion: The framework aims to balance detection quality, resource cost, and response timing, but requires experimental validation.

title: Quantified Propositional Calculi And Narrow Implicit Proofs
authors: Neil Thapen Pavel Pudl\'ak
abstract: ArXiv:2606.10535v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In the implicit version of a propositional proof system Q, we work with Q-proofs that are not written down directly, but are succinctly encoded by circuits. Thus implicit Q-proofs are potentially exponentially shorter than usual Q-proofs. We study narrow implicit proofs, a restricted version of this notion, in which lines in the encoded proof can only have polynomial size. We use a cut-elimination construction to show that G_{i+1} is equivalent to narrow implicit G_i, for i >= 1, where G_i is the extension of Frege allowing reasoning with Sigma^q_i quantified propositional formulas. We show that G_1 is equivalent to implicit resolution.
tldr: The paper studies implicit propositional proofs and their equivalence to quantified propositional calculi, focusing on proof complexity rather than quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: To understand the relationship between implicit proof systems and quantified propositional calculi, and to show that narrow implicit proofs can be exponentially shorter than standard proofs.
method: Uses cut-elimination constructions to prove equivalences between different proof systems, such as G_{i+1} and narrow implicit G_i, and G_1 with implicit resolution.
result: Establishes that G_{i+1} is equivalent to narrow implicit G_i for i >= 1, and G_1 is equivalent to implicit resolution.
conclusion: The work contributes to proof complexity theory but has no connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Snaproot: Decentralized File Integrity Verification Using Blockchain-Anchored Cryptographic Hashing
authors: Tarkan Yavas Arslan Br\"omme
abstract: ArXiv:2606.10625v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The rapid growth of digital content has made reliable integrity verification increasingly important. Existing solutions rely either on centralized authorities, which introduce trust dependencies and single points of failure, or on decentralized storage systems that incur prohibitive resource overhead. In this paper, we present snaproot, a lightweight system that implements the hash-anchoring paradigm of Haber and Stornetta on the Solana blockchain to provide efficient, decentralized file integrity verification. snaproot generates a SHA-256 hash of a file and stores it immutably on-chain as a permanent reference record. Verification is performed by recomputing the hash and comparing it to the stored value, yielding a deterministic binary outcome. We describe a four-tier trust architecture comprising three realized tiers and one prospective tier for long-term persistence beyond the lifetime of any single blockchain. We present a formal threat model, a security analysis grounded in the second-preimage resistance of SHA-256, and an empirical evaluation on Solana Devnet across file sizes from 1 KB to 500 MB. A central conceptual contribution is the explicit separation between existence proof, the key-independent claim that a file existed at a given time, and authorship proof, the key-dependent binding between a record and a specific wallet identity. This separation allows existence guarantees to survive key loss while preserving stronger authorship claims where keys are retained. We position snaproot against OpenTimestamps, OriginStamp, and Chainpoint and discuss limitations with respect to pre-registration manipulation and AI-generated content.
tldr: This paper presents a blockchain-based file integrity verification system using SHA-256 hashing on Solana.
motivation: Existing centralized and decentralized integrity solutions suffer from trust dependencies or high resource overhead.
method: The system generates a SHA-256 hash of a file and stores it immutably on the Solana blockchain; verification recomputes the hash and compares it to the stored value.
result: Empirical evaluation on Solana Devnet shows feasibility across file sizes from 1 KB to 500 MB, with a formal threat model and security analysis.
conclusion: Snaproot provides lightweight, decentralized integrity verification with a clear separation between existence and authorship proofs.

title: Post-Quantum Secure Federated DeFi For Inclusive Banking
authors: Swati Sachan, Dale Fickett, Richard Buchinger, Theo Miller
abstract: ArXiv:2606.10658v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent advances in error-corrected qubits have accelerated the timeline for practical quantum computing. It poses a threat to cryptographic primitives used to secure financial systems, government infrastructure, communication networks, and DeFi (Decentralized Finance) ecosystems. This paper introduces a post-quantum secure federated DeFi framework that enables inter-bank collaboration to improve the inclusivity of individuals underserved by local lenders due to limited financial histories. Multiple banks contribute encrypted information batches to a virtual server, where lattice-based Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) enables end-to-end homomorphic computation. The server fuses local data-driven probabilistic assessments, expert beliefs, and verifiable evidence generated by the NASA-IBM Prithvi Geospatial Foundation Model (GFM), in encrypted format. Decentralized technologies are employed to ensure tamper-proof evidence and auditable accountability for all encrypted data exchanges between institutions and the server. The framework is tested on agricultural lending decisions for rural borrowers in Virginia.
tldr: A post-quantum secure federated DeFi framework using lattice-based FHE and geospatial AI for inclusive banking.
motivation: To protect DeFi systems from quantum threats and improve financial inclusion for underserved borrowers.
method: Combines lattice-based fully homomorphic encryption, federated learning, and NASA-IBM Prithvi Geospatial Foundation Model for encrypted data fusion.
result: Demonstrates feasibility on agricultural lending decisions in rural Virginia.
conclusion: The framework offers quantum-secure, privacy-preserving inter-bank collaboration for inclusive finance.

result: They constructed a phase diagram for the methane-helium binary system up to ~50 GPa, identifying several phase transitions and immiscibility regions.
conclusion: The results provide essential data for planetary interior models and reveal complex phase behavior in simple molecular mixtures under extreme conditions.

title: Order And Disorder At The Atomic Scale: Microscopy Applied To Semiconductors
authors: Enrico Di Russo, Tom Verstijnen, Paul Koenraad, Konstantinos Pantzas, Gilles Patriarche, And Lorenzo Rigutti
abstract:
Author(s): Enrico Di Russo, Tom Verstijnen, Paul Koenraad, Konstantinos Pantzas, Gilles Patriarche, and Lorenzo Rigutti

Atomic-scale details, especially those of disorder, are important for material properties, especially in semiconductors, but they are also extremely difficult to measure. Real-space methods can give direct access to this information, but typically, that access is limited. This review reports the application of three real-space techniques for measuring disorder to compound semiconductor materials: scanning tunneling microscopy, transmission electron microscopy, and atom-probe microscopy. Where possible, it emphasizes cases in which the probes have been combined to achieve a more complete picture of the defects.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 025006] Published Thu Jun 26, 2025.
tldr: A review of real-space microscopy techniques for measuring atomic-scale disorder in semiconductors.
motivation: Atomic-scale disorder critically affects semiconductor properties but is difficult to measure; the paper reviews three real-space techniques to address this challenge.
method: The authors review scanning tunneling microscopy, transmission electron microscopy, and atom-probe microscopy, emphasizing combined use for a complete defect picture.
result: The review highlights capabilities and limitations of each technique and cases where they complement each other.
conclusion: Combining multiple real-space probes provides a more comprehensive understanding of atomic-scale disorder in semiconductors.

title: Quantum Physics Of Stars
authors: M. Wiescher, C. A. Bertulani, C. R. Brune, R. J. Deboer, A. Diaz-Torres, L. R. Gasques, K. Langanke, P. Navrátil, W. Nazarewicz, J. Okołowicz, D. R. Phillips, M. Płoszajczak, S. Quaglioni, And A. Tumino
abstract:
Author(s): M. Wiescher, C. A. Bertulani, C. R. Brune, R. J. deBoer, A. Diaz-Torres, L. R. Gasques, K. Langanke, P. Navrátil, W. Nazarewicz, J. Okołowicz, D. R. Phillips, M. Płoszajczak, S. Quaglioni, and A. Tumino

There are many nuclear reactions that are of central importance for stellar burning and element formation. In typical stars, these reactions take place at very low energy, and many of them have very small rates, making it difficult to measure them directly in the laboratory. On the theoretical side, the low-energy regime is governed by quantum-mechanical phenomena like tunneling, near-threshold resonances, and interference effects. This review summarizes the state of the art in the theory of low-energy nuclear reactions in stars and describes new ideas for studying these reactions on Earth.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 025003] Published Tue May 27, 2025.
tldr: A review of low-energy nuclear reactions in stars, focusing on quantum tunneling and resonances, with no connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.
motivation: Nuclear reactions in stars are crucial for stellar burning and element formation, but many have very small rates at low energies, making direct measurement difficult.
method: The paper reviews theoretical approaches to low-energy nuclear reactions, including quantum tunneling, near-threshold resonances, and interference effects, and discusses experimental techniques to study them on Earth.
result: Summarizes the state of the art in low-energy nuclear reaction theory and proposes new ideas for laboratory measurements.
conclusion: Quantum mechanical phenomena dominate stellar nuclear reactions, and further theoretical and experimental work is needed to understand them.

title: The Need For Optoacoustic Microscopy
authors: Ludwig Englert, Dominik Jüstel, And Vasilis Ntziachristos
abstract:
Author(s): Ludwig Englert, Dominik Jüstel, and Vasilis Ntziachristos

Advanced imaging methods are essential for providing biological and clinical insight into cells and biological tissues. Optoacoustic imaging is one such method in which cells or tissues absorb short laser pulses and the resulting rise in temperature creates tiny ultrasound waves that can be detected by ultrasonic detectors placed outside the specimen. This noninvasive technique has the ability to look at optical contrast that is millimeters and even centimeters deep with high resolution. This review discusses the basic physics, how the method impacts biological and clinical research, and the latest developments in multimodal microscopy and imaging combining optical and optoacoustic techniques.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 015005] Published Tue Mar 04, 2025.
tldr: This review discusses optoacoustic microscopy, a biomedical imaging technique that uses laser-induced ultrasound to image deep into tissues.
motivation: Advanced imaging methods are needed to provide biological and clinical insight into cells and tissues at depth with high resolution.
method: The paper reviews the basic physics of optoacoustic imaging, where short laser pulses are absorbed by tissue, causing a temperature rise that generates ultrasound waves detected by external sensors.
result: Optoacoustic imaging can achieve high-resolution imaging at depths of millimeters to centimeters, and recent developments combine it with optical techniques for multimodal microscopy.
conclusion: Optoacoustic microscopy is a powerful noninvasive imaging tool with significant potential for biological and clinical research.

title: Wannier-function Software Ecosystem For Materials Simulations
authors: Antimo Marrazzo, Sophie Beck, Elena R. Margine, Nicola Marzari, Arash A. Mostofi, Junfeng Qiao, Ivo Souza, Stepan S. Tsirkin, Jonathan R. Yates, And Giovanni Pizzi
abstract:
Author(s): Antimo Marrazzo, Sophie Beck, Elena R. Margine, Nicola Marzari, Arash A. Mostofi, Junfeng Qiao, Ivo Souza, Stepan S. Tsirkin, Jonathan R. Yates, and Giovanni Pizzi

The description of the electronic structure in terms of extended Bloch states has made it possible to understand and calculate many properties in condensed-matter physics. However, understanding and insight often require a local description, and Wannier functions provide an exact and insightful map of extended reciprocal-space Bloch states into localized real-space orbitals. Applications range far and wide, from ultra-accurate integrations to topological invariants, and their widespread uptake by the electronic-structure community has resulted in a growing and interoperable ecosystem of methods and associated software tools. This review provides a description of this ecosystem that has now become a major instrument for the electronic-structure community in its pursuit of understanding, discovering, and designing materials.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 96, 045008] Published Mon Dec 23, 2024.
tldr: A review of the Wannier-function software ecosystem for materials simulations.
motivation: To provide a comprehensive overview of the methods and tools based on Wannier functions for electronic structure calculations.
method: The paper surveys various software packages and their interoperability, focusing on the generation and use of maximally localized Wannier functions.
result: It describes the ecosystem's capabilities for computing band structures, topological invariants, and other properties.
conclusion: The Wannier-function ecosystem is a major instrument for the electronic-structure community, enabling accurate and insightful materials simulations.

title: Distinguishing Near- Versus Off-critical Phase Behaviors Of Intrinsically Disordered Proteins
authors: Gaurav Mitra, Souradeep Ghosh, Kiersten M Ruff, Ruoyao Zhang, Gaurav Chauhan And Rohit V Pappu
abstract: Intrinsically disordered prion-like low complexity domains (PLCDs) drive phase transitions that underlie the biogenesis of many biomolecular condensates. Here, we report results from large-scale Monte Carlo simulations on lattices aided by computations of Binder cumulants and rigorous finite-size scaling. These approaches enable accurate mapping of the critical regime and computations of the full binodal of an archetypal PLCD. This weakly associating polymer undergoes phase separation coupled to percolation. Between the lowest temperature and the critical point, the concentrations along the left arm of the binodal vary by four orders of magnitude. The overlap line intersects the left arm of the binodal well below the critical point. This, taken together with the intersection of the percolation line and the left arm of the binodal, leads to demarcation of the binodal into three regimes. Regime I is farthest from the critical point. Here, the coexisting dilute phase is akin to a gas of dispersed polymers. The dilute arm of the binodal lies above the overlap line in Regimes II and III. Here, the semidilute nature of dilute phases enables clustering of polymers that is enhanced by intermolecular associations. The coexisting dense phases form confined percolated networks in Regimes I and II. In Regime III, which is closest to the critical point, the dense phase becomes unconfined and fragmented, and the system is defined by two interconnected, system-spanning networks. In addition to mapping the critical point accurately, we evaluated methods for identifying the theta temperature. We find that scaling approaches based on assumptions from two-parameter theories for homopolymers yield erroneous estimates of the theta temperature of an archetypal PLCD. Accurate estimation of the theta temperature requires direct calculation of the temperature dependence of the two-body interaction coefficient. We discuss implications for inferring solvent quality from scaling analysis of segmental distances of disordered proteins.
tldr: This paper uses Monte Carlo simulations and finite-size scaling to study phase behavior of intrinsically disordered proteins, focusing on critical vs. off-critical regimes.
motivation: Understanding phase transitions of prion-like low complexity domains is important for biomolecular condensate biogenesis, but the paper is purely biophysical with no quantum or information-theoretic content.
method: Large-scale Monte Carlo simulations on lattices with Binder cumulants and finite-size scaling to map binodals and percolation lines.
result: The binodal is divided into three regimes based on overlap and percolation lines; scaling approaches from homopolymer theory give erroneous theta temperature estimates.
conclusion: Accurate theta temperature estimation requires direct calculation of the two-body interaction coefficient, with implications for solvent quality inference in disordered proteins.

title: Electric-field-driven Nanoconfinement And The 5–120 Nm Stability Regime Of Piezoelectric Β-glycine
authors: Kexin Zhang And Zhengbao Yang
abstract: Piezoelectric β-glycine is a promising molecular crystal, yet its controlled preparation remains challenging. Current nanoconfinement strategies, which rely primarily on rigid templates or simulations, cannot reliably capture the intrinsic confinement regime that leads to β-phase formation. Here, we propose electric-field-driven nanoconfinement as a one-step, continuous, and interface-free approach to investigate glycine crystallization and to define the confinement regime that yields the β-phase. We produced glycine nanoparticles via electrohydrodynamic spraying under a direct current field, automatically varying the spraying height to modulate nanoconfinement during nucleation and growth. Structural, morphological, and piezoelectric characterizations reveal that pure β-glycine forms within a crystal radius range of 5–120 nm. By integrating these findings with thermodynamic and kinetic analysis, we elucidate the mechanism of β-phase formation and construct a crystallization phase map that delineates the confinement conditions necessary for its stabilization. This work identifies the critical nanoconfinement parameters for accessing piezoelectric β-glycine and provides fundamental insights into polymorph control in molecular crystalline materials.
tldr: This paper studies electric-field-driven nanoconfinement to stabilize piezoelectric β-glycine, a molecular crystal, with no connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.
motivation: Controlled preparation of piezoelectric β-glycine is challenging; existing nanoconfinement methods cannot reliably capture the regime leading to β-phase formation.
method: Electric-field-driven nanoconfinement via electrohydrodynamic spraying under DC field, varying spraying height to modulate confinement during nucleation and growth.
result: Pure β-glycine forms within a crystal radius range of 5–120 nm; a crystallization phase map is constructed.
conclusion: The work identifies critical nanoconfinement parameters for accessing piezoelectric β-glycine and provides insights into polymorph control in molecular crystals.

title: Mean Field Game Model Of The Impact Of Reductions In Support On Faculty Research Activity
authors: Robert A. Brownahttps://ror.org/05qwgg493faculty Of Computing & Data Sciences, Boston University, Boston, MA 02215
